EgoStream: A Diagnostic Benchmark for
Streaming Episodic Memory in Egocentric Vision

Rosario Forte    Giuseppe Lando    Antonino Furnari Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science Affiliation: University of Catania Affiliation: Catania, Italy Email: rosario.forte@phd.unict.it Email: giuseppe.lando@studium.unict.it Email: antonino.furnari@unict.it
Abstract

Continuous episodic memory is a core capability for autonomous agents operating in dynamic, real-world environments, yet current streaming video benchmarks provide limited tools for diagnosing what models remember and for how long. We introduce EgoStream, a diagnostic benchmark for streaming episodic memory evaluation in egocentric vision. EgoStream organizes 2,250 curated questions along seven cognitive dimensions: detail, spatial, temporal, event, social, causal, and prospective memory. We introduce the Answer Validity Window (AVW), which specifies the temporal span an answer remains valid as the observed scene evolves. This allows us to expand the questions into 8,528 recall-conditioned evaluations, enabling controlled testing from instant to ultra-long-term recall while separating genuine model forgetting from natural world-state changes. We rigorously establish baseline performance through a unified streaming MLLM framework that compares several state-of-the-art memory-management mechanisms, covering sliding windows, attention sinks, KV-cache pruning, merging, and offloading. Experiments within a unified Qwen3-VL backbone reveal that comparable aggregate accuracies mask starkly different memory profiles. For instance, token pruning preserves fine-grained details and temporal structure significantly better than token merging, while quantized offloading rescues ultra-long-term recall. Ultimately, all mechanisms operate well below real-time (>1s per frame), and top performing methods ceil at about 45% accuracy, exposing critical gaps in current architectures. EgoStream provides the diagnostic testbed needed to close these gaps.

1 Introduction

To operate successfully in the physical world, an autonomous agent must store and recall episodic events across both short and long temporal horizons Tulving and others (1972); Tulving (2002); Clayton et al. (2001). For visual embodied AI systems, streaming egocentric video offers a natural testbed for studying continuous memory, as it captures first-person experience as it unfolds over time Grauman et al. (2022); Bärmann and Waibel (2022), unlike detached exocentric media such as movies or surveillance footage. This makes the egocentric domain ideal for real-world memory tasks, including wearable assistants and embodied agents that must provide context-aware support Grauman et al. (2022); Plizzari et al. (2024); Yang et al. (2025a); Mangalam et al. (2023); Perrett et al. (2025). In this setting, egocentric assistants must answer questions about past events (e.g., whether the user locked the door or where an object was placed), processing observations incrementally and maintaining a compact memory under bounded resources. This makes memory in egocentric vision particularly challenging: relevant evidence may appear long before it is queried, requiring the model to decide what to retain during streaming perception.

Despite recent progress in egocentric Video Question Answering (VideoQA), existing offline benchmarks still provide only a limited view of episodic memory Grauman et al. (2022); Mangalam et al. (2023); Di and Xie (2024); Chen et al. (2025a); Plizzari et al. (2025); Perrett et al. (2025). While they have substantially advanced long-form understanding and reasoning, they do not isolate memory as a measurable variable. The temporal distance between the supporting evidence and the query is rarely controlled, and evaluation does not distinguish what information must be remembered, how long it must be retained, or when a previously correct answer becomes invalid in a changing environment. Recent online and streaming benchmarks move closer to this setting Lin et al. (2024); Niu et al. (2025); Xiong et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025a), but primarily measure online responsiveness or aggregate accuracy rather than providing a diagnostic account of memory quality. Consequently, models with very different memory profiles may obtain similar scores. One may preserve coarse event gist while forgetting object locations, whereas another may retain short-term spatial details but fail at long-horizon causal recall. This flattened assessment makes it difficult to determine which forms of episodic information are preserved by current streaming models and which degrade first. This limitation has led to a proliferation of memory-management methods that address streaming constraints  Xu et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2023); Li et al. (2024); Bolya et al. (2023); Yang et al. (2025b); Kim et al. (2025). Evaluating these methods solely through aggregate performance masks the qualitative trade-offs induced by their architectural choices. We argue that streaming memory evaluation should measure not only whether a model answers correctly, but also what kind of episodic information is retained and for how long.

To support progress in visual episodic memory systems, we introduce EgoStream (Figure 1), a new benchmark curated from existing egocentric VideoQA datasets Di and Xie (2024); Chen et al. (2025a); Plizzari et al. (2025); Perrett et al. (2025); Yang et al. (2025a) and reorganized through a cognitive- and application-oriented framework. Drawing inspiration from cognitive accounts of episodic memory and related memory functions Tulving and others (1972); Tulving (2002); Burgess et al. (2002); Friedman (1993); Radvansky and Zacks (2014); Trabasso and Van Den Broek (1985); McDaniel and Einstein (2007), we curate queries to test seven dimensions of memory: detail, spatial, temporal, event, social, causal, and prospective memory. To support a consistent evaluation of memory retention over time, we introduce the concept of Answer Validity Window (AVW)—a temporal span indicating the timeframe during which a specific past observation remains factually true before being overturned by subsequent events. Because continuous egocentric vision is dynamic, annotating AVWs ensures that forgetting is not conflated with scene evolution. Each question is then evaluated across instant recall, short-term memory, long-term memory, and ultra-long-term memory. This organization is also consistent with classic studies showing that memory should be evaluated across controlled retention intervals Ebbinghaus (1885); Murre and Dros (2015); Dudai (2004); Moscovitch et al. (2006b).

To establish a picture of current progress we implement core memory-management strategies (e.g., sliding windows, attention sinks, token pruning, token merging) within a unified MLLM architecture. This controlled setup reveals that similar aggregate accuracy can hide distinct memory profiles, with policies preserving different semantic information and degrading differently across recall horizons. Our experiments reveal that established state-of-the-art memory management mechanisms exhibit only marginal performance differences when evaluated within our unified framework and that aggregate accuracies mask divergent memory profiles. For instance, token pruning preserves fine-grained details and temporal structure significantly better than token merging. This highlights the need to evaluate streaming memory by the specific episodic information preserved and its temporal accessibility, rather than just average accuracy.

Our contributions are threefold. 1) We introduce EgoStream, a benchmark for streaming episodic memory in egocentric vision, built from five egocentric datasets and comprising 2,250 validated memory questions expanded into 8,528 recall-conditioned evaluations. 2) We organize episodic memory along seven semantic dimensions and introduce the Answer Validity Window (AVW) to measure temporal retention as the world evolves. 3) We provide a unified streaming MLLM framework for the controlled comparison of memory-management techniques. Annotations, code, and evaluation scripts are shared through the provided anonymous GitHub repository.

2 Related Work

Episodic Memory in Egocentric Vision Episodic memory in egocentric vision initially focused on offline temporal localization Grauman et al. (2022) and grounded QA Bärmann and Waibel (2022); Di and Xie (2024); Jiang et al. (2023). Recognizing the continuous nature of first-person experience, recent efforts have shifted toward online streaming. While some approaches track memory through object-centric representations Manigrasso et al. (2026); Goletto et al. (2024); Fan et al. (2025), VideoQA emerge as a suitable protocol for episodic retrieval, accelerated by MLLMs Di and Xie (2024). This shift has driven diverse continuous memory strategies, including dynamic KV-cache retrieval Di et al. (2025), cache compression Kim et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025b), and hierarchical memory reuse Zhang et al. (2026); Zhang et al. (2025); Xu et al. (2025). However, these works treat streaming memory as a modeling challenge, evaluated implicitly through end-task VideoQA. Repeated stream queries directly probe whether an observed fact is retained, forgotten, or superseded. EgoStream builds on this by making episodic recall the primary evaluation target, not merely a means for downstream VideoQA.

VideoQA and Streaming Benchmarks. Existing benchmarks have significantly advanced long-form video comprehension Song et al. (2023), with recent egocentric datasets specializing this setting for first-person reasoning. These works cover a broad spectrum of abilities, including long-form QA Mangalam et al. (2023); Ye et al. (2025); Zhou et al. (2025), temporal grounding and multi-step reasoning Di and Xie (2024); Chen et al. (2025a); Plizzari et al. (2025), and fine-grained daily-life assistance Perrett et al. (2025); Yang et al. (2025a). In parallel, streaming-oriented benchmarks like StreamingBench Lin et al. (2024) and OVO-Bench Niu et al. (2025) evaluate online responsiveness by posing queries during continuous video streams rather than assuming full offline access. Despite this progress, memory remains an implicit byproduct of broader video understanding or online interaction. As shown in Table 1, prior benchmarks address aspects like egocentric perception, streaming evaluation, or temporal reasoning. However, none jointly provide an explicit memory taxonomy, Answer Validity Windows, and controlled recall regimes. EgoStream addresses this gap by turning streaming episodic memory into a specific, diagnostic evaluation target.

Streaming Memory Architectures in Video LLMs. To bound memory growth in continuous video streams, recent Video-LLMs employ mechanisms such as recency-based retention Xiao et al. (2024), KV-cache pruning Zhang et al. (2023); Li et al. (2024); Kim et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025b), token merging Bolya et al. (2023); Zhang et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2025b), and external retrieval Di et al. (2025). These methods reduce spatial and temporal redundancy Kim et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025b); Yang et al. (2025b), often aided by quantization Chen et al. (2025b).While they improve latency and efficiency, they are typically evaluated only via aggregate online accuracy, leaving unclear what each policy preserves and how abilities decay over time. EgoStream addresses this by evaluating representative memory families under a unified backbone, enabling controlled analysis of what streaming models remember, for how long, and which dimensions fail first.

3 The EgoStream Benchmark

3.1 Source Curation and Initial Set of Questions

We curate question-answer sets from five egocentric VideoQA datasets: Ego4D Episodic Memory VQA Bärmann and Waibel (2022), EgoLife Yang et al. (2025a), EgoTempo Plizzari et al. (2025), Multi-Hop EgoQA Chen et al. (2025a), and HD-EPIC Perrett et al. (2025). These sources cover complementary aspects of egocentric perception, including episodic memory and temporal localization, long-context life assistance, fine-grained temporal reasoning, multi-hop grounded reasoning, and kitchen activity recognition. To unify these annotations under a streaming evaluation protocol, we apply a standardized curation pipeline. First, we ensure that all queries are explicit retrospective memory probes. Questions from Ego4D Bärmann and Waibel (2022), EgoLife Yang et al. (2025a), and EgoTempo Yang et al. (2025a) are already suitable, while those from HD-EPIC Perrett et al. (2025) and Multi-Hop EgoQA Chen et al. (2025a) are rewritten using Gemini 3.1 Team (2025), e.g., “What is the best description for why the person performed the action <tip bowl> in video 1?” is rewritten into “What was the person trying to achieve by tipping the bowl?”

To support a standardized 44-way multiple-choice evaluation, we use Gemini 3.1 Team (2025) to generate three plausible distractors for open-ended datasets, namely EgoTempo Plizzari et al. (2025) and Multi-Hop EgoQA Chen et al. (2025a). We then apply an LLM-based quality-control step to remove ambiguous, trivial, or overly similar negatives, while preserving the original multiple-choice options for the remaining datasets (see Appendix A.1). Finally, each question is attached the temporal segment containing the visual evidence needed to infer the correct answer, which we refer to as the evidence moment (see Appendix A.2). These annotations are inherited from the source datasets. This yields 2,6342,634 QA sets, that undergo a comprehensive human validation step. Annotators manually verify the accuracy of the question-answer pairs and the plausibility of the distractors (See Appendix A.3). This step filters out roughly 12% of the initial pool, yielding 2,3352,335 human-verified, temporally grounded video QA instances.

3.2 The Cognitive Dimensions of Episodic Memory

EgoStream isolates what a model remembers by partitioning queries into seven dimensions grounded in foundational cognitive theory Tulving and others (1972); Tulving (2002). We structure this taxonomy around the natural “W-question” framework of human recall. Building upon the core episodic triad of what, where, and when Clayton et al. (2001); Burgess et al. (2002); Friedman (1993), we incorporate expanded dimensions critical for embodied agents: procedural actions (how) Radvansky and Zacks (2014), social context (who) Grunewald and Schweizer (2026); Stewardson et al. (2023), causal reasoning (why) Trabasso and Van Den Broek (1985), and prospective intentions (what next) McDaniel and Einstein (2007). These categories are defined and summarized with examples in Table 2.

Because episodic queries frequently involve overlapping cognitive demands (for instance, “Who was with me when I operated the machine?” contains both social and temporal cues) we assign each question one primary label and zero or more secondary tags, following the taxonomy in Table 2. To efficiently scale this process, we employed an iterative Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) annotation pipeline (see Appendix A.4). After this process 8585 questions were discarded for not aligning to any of the category or being unclear, leaving 2,2502,250 valid questions (comprising 578 from Multi-Hop EgoQA Chen et al. (2025a), 498 from Ego4D Bärmann and Waibel (2022), 433 from EgoLife Yang et al. (2025a), 425 from EgoTempo Plizzari et al. (2025), and 316 from HD-EPIC Perrett et al. (2025)). Figure 2 reports the distribution of primary categories and across data subsets. For reference, the text-only baseline obtains an average accuracy of 25.42% demonstrating no stronger text bias See Appendix A.8 for a breakdown by semantic categories.

3.3 The Answer Validity Window and Recall Regimes

Time is the second fundamental dimension of episodic memory recall. To systematically evaluate this axis, we introduce the concept of Answer Validity Window (AVW), i.e., the precise temporal interval during which a question’s original answer remains semantically valid after all its supporting visually relevant evidence has been observed. Identifying this validity window is critical in continuous egocentric streams, where facts are inherently transient. An initially correct answer to a query such as “Is the glass full?” can rapidly become obsolete due to subsequent actions (e.g., drinking), object displacements (e.g., moving the glass), or broader scene evolutions. We annotate the AVW using the temporal structure of each source dataset. For EgoTempo, the AVW is 00, as questions are asked at the end of the trimmed input video. For Ego4D-VQA and Multi-Hop EgoQA, it spans from the end of the evidence moment to the end of the provided clip, while for EgoLife it extends to the long-term query time defined by the original dataset. For HD-EPIC, where validity intervals are not directly provided, we use Gemini 3.1 Team (2025) to identify narration chunks in which the answer is observable and derive the AVW by trimming duplicate evidence around the ground-truth moment. All automatically derived annotations were manually reviewed for consistency. See Appendix A.5 for more details.

Associating an AVW to each question enables us to evaluate episodic memory at multiple recall regimes, reminiscent of classic memory testing paradigms Ebbinghaus (1885); Murre and Dros (2015). In practice, we sample multiple query times between the end of the relevant moment and the end of the validity interval, ensuring that forgetting is not conflated with answer invalidation caused by scene evolution. Drawing on established memory consolidation timescales Dudai (2004); Moscovitch et al. (2006b), application-oriented considerations Plizzari et al. (2024), and empirical support in our data (see Figure 3), we define seven recall regimes spanning a log-scaled progression. Table 3 reports the proposed recall regimes and terminology, with supporting references from psychology and the empirical distribution of memory categories within each temporal window.

Given the AVW annotations, we expand each curated question into one or more recall evaluations. Each question is first evaluated in the instant regime, immediately after the evidence moment, to measure whether the model can answer before memory decay becomes a factor. We then sample additional query times within the AVW according to our recall-regime taxonomy, with distribution parameters adjusted to match the empirical temporal structure of the source data. This produces a realistic set of recall delays across short- and long-horizon settings, yielding 8,5288,528 question-recall evaluations. Further details are provided in Appendix A.6.

3.4 Evaluation Protocol and Metrics

To establish EgoStream as a standardized reference for future researchers, we explicitly define inference rules and scoring metrics, as well as provide scripts to standardize evaluation.

Streaming Constraints. The benchmark strictly enforces a streaming inference protocol. Models must process the video sequentially: a query issued at timestamp tt must be answered utilizing only the visual content observed up to tt. Models are expected to maintain a compact internal representation of the past, avoiding to store raw video frames in an unbounded buffer to be reprocessed at query time. The visual processing required to form this memory must be purely query-agnostic, as the evaluation query is only revealed to the model at the exact moment of recall.

Evaluation. EgoStream evaluates models by submitting the 2,2502,250 valid questions across their applicable recall regimes, resulting in 8,5288,528 individual inferences. Performance is assessed via standard accuracy (broken down across semantic categories and recall regimes) on the 44-way multiple-choice setup, with a chance-level baseline corresponding to 0.250.25. While individual methods are free to choose their specific system prompts, we utilize a unified prompt and answer-selection scheme for fair comparisons (see Appendix A.7). Methods are evaluated under limited memory budgets, and reporting the average processing time per frame.

4 A Unified Framework for Streaming Episodic Memory

Current evaluations of state-of-the-art models often confound memory mechanisms with orthogonal design choices, such as varying vision encoders or pre-training mixtures. To enable controlled diagnostic evaluations, we introduce a unified streaming Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) framework that isolates memory management as an independent variable. Instantiated on a frozen Qwen3-VL Bai et al. (2025) backbone, our framework adapts to streaming VideoQA by continuously appending newly encoded visual tokens to the KV cache. This enables incremental video processing without recomputing past contexts at every query. By keeping the encoder, projector, LLM decoder, and prompting scheme strictly fixed, we provide a testbed for benchmarking distinct memory techniques. Our unified pipeline allows us to replicate popular state-of-the-art streaming video understanding approaches Chen et al. (2025b); Kim et al. (2025); Yang et al. (2025b); Xu et al. (2025); Di et al. (2025) on a plug-and-play memory manager that operates directly in KV-cache.

Figure 4 illustrates our unified streaming memory framework, detailing the cache organization, memory management, and update dynamics. The core principle of our approach is to restrict memory operations—such as merging, pruning, and offloading—strictly to historical visual evidence. This ensures that both the system prompt and the most recent observations are always preserved. As the video stream progresses, the memory manager continuously enforces a strict budget on the active cache. At question time, the model answers using this curated cache, drawing upon the most relevant available evidence selected from live blocks or, when retrieval is enabled, offloaded memory.

4.1 Memory Management Strategies

In the following, we detail the main Memory Management Strategies evaluated within our framework, which draw upon established techniques from prior KV-cache and streaming-video memory research. See Appendix B for more details.

Protected cache regions. Following attention-sink and streaming-inference methods, which show that structural tokens are critical for stable long-context decoding Xu et al. (2025); Kim et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2023), we preserve the system prompt as fixed sink tokens (SINK). We also reserve a small protected region for the most recent visual tokens, denoted hat tokens (HAT), analogous to recent-token budgets in KV-cache reduction and streaming methods Zhang et al. (2023); Xiao et al. (2024); Kim et al. (2025). This organization (Figure 4a) preserves instruction-following and grounding for recent content, restricting memory management to the mutable historical cache.

Intra-frame reduction. Treating the mutable cache as an undifferentiated pool can discard temporal coverage. To prevent this, we evaluate frame-local reducers that compress redundant evidence within individual frames (Figure 4b). We apply pruning or merging based on four criteria: cosine redundancy (INTRA-COS) between adjacent key states; pseudo-attention salience (INTRA-PA) to discard low-attended tokens Chen et al. (2025b); value-norm ranking (INTRA-VN) to prune low-norm states Kim et al. (2025); and sink-guided cross-attention (INTRA-CS) to remove tokens least attended by the system prompt Yang et al. (2025b).

Inter-frame reduction. Adjacent egocentric frames often share highly redundant content, enabling temporal compression. Following prior streaming-video methods, our memory manager compares neighboring frames in the mutable cache to prune redundant tokens when the budget is exceeded. We evaluate two cross-frame reducers: cosine redundancy (INTER-COS), which matches tokens using cosine similarity Chen et al. (2025b), and pseudo-attention salience (INTER-PA), which uses cross-frame pseudo-attention to estimate token importance Yang et al. (2025b) (Figure 4b).

Residual overflow policy. When the reduced cache still exceeds its budget, we apply an overflow policy (Figure 4b): either FIFO, which discards the oldest tokens Xiao et al. (2024), or offloading (OFFLOAD), which preserves excess chunks on disk for retrieval at question time via cosine similarity Di et al. (2025). To minimize storage costs, we also evaluate an int8 quantized offloading variant (Q-OFF) Chen et al. (2025b).

5 Experiments and Results

We evaluate the capabilities of current streaming architectures on EgoStream via a controlled diagnostic evaluation using our unified framework, an analysis of semantic profiles and temporal decay, and a comparison of state-of-the-art models. Configuration and hardware detailed in Appendix C.1.

5.1 Controlled Diagnostic Evaluation

Table 4 shows that while aggregate performance gaps among memory strategies are narrow, critical variations exist in what is retained and for how long. Established methods like ReKV Di et al. (2025) and StreamVLM Xu et al. (2025) remain highly competitive, performing on par with recent approaches like InfiniPot-V Kim et al. (2025). No single method strictly dominates, showing that some are locally optimal for spatial or temporal retention (Rows 4, 4), while others (Rows 4, 4) balance accuracy and processing time. These trade-offs reveal key trends that can guide the design of future streaming architectures.

The role of SINKand HATtokens. The naive Sliding Window (FIFO, Row 4) yields the lowest accuracy. Adding SINKtokens (StreamVLM Xu et al. (2025), Row 4) boosts semantic and temporal averages from 29.53%/28.33% to 44.74%/39.05%, with negligible latency change (1.05s to 1.07s). This confirms that preserving system prompts is essential for stable inference Xiao et al. (2024). Including HATtokens adds a small benefit under the same policy, increasing semantic/temporal accuracy from 44.38%/40.23% to 45.19%/40.43% (Rows 4 and 4). These results show the value of protecting structural context.

Merge vs. Prune. PRUNE mechanisms consistently outperform token MERGE. For INTRA-PA, pruning (Row 4) beats merging (Row 4) 45.12% to 41.87%. Discarding redundant tokens preserves episodic details better than averaging, which blurs fine-grained evidence (see DETL). While using a hybrid PRUNE/MERGE approach (Row 4) closes this gap (up to 45.97%), it drastically increases processing time (5.56s vs. ∼\sim2.5s for pure intra-merging).

Optimal in-memory strategies. Combining intra- and inter-frame reduction yields the best streaming policies. The hybrid PRUNE INTRA-PA INTER-COS(Row 4) provides the strongest overall trade-off between semantic and temporal recall (45.19%/40.43%), excelling in Spatial and Detail memory. Blending local salience filtering with cross-frame redundancy checks optimally preserves visual anchors. However, this peak accuracy incurs the highest processing time (5.51s), more expensive than variants like PRUNE INTRA-COS(Row 4, 2.28s).

Offloading. OFFLOAD keeps evicted memory on disk, but alone is weaker than in-memory pruning. Row 4 reaches 40.99% / 36.83% with 2.0966 GB×\timesmin. Q-OFF halves storage to 1.0515 GB×\timesmin and improves accuracy (Row 4: 41.63% / 38.77%, 1.59s), while StreamingTOM (Row 4) obtains better results combining low-salience tokens PRUNE+Q-OFF for 42.86% / 39.93%, gaining 34.21% for Ultra-Long recall and only 0.4847 GB×\timesmin.

5.2 State-of-the-Art Streaming Models

When comparing state-of-the-art streaming architectures under our unified KV-cache framework, distinct accuracy–latency trade-offs emerge rather than a strict ranking (Table 4). StreamVLM Xu et al. (2025) serves as the strongest low-latency baseline, proving that protecting SINK tokens yields high semantic (44.74%) and temporal (39.05%) accuracy with minimal overhead (1.07s). For tasks requiring higher fidelity, token pruning models like StreamMem Yang et al. (2025b), InfiniPot-V Kim et al. (2025), and StreamTOM Chen et al. (2025b) (without offloading) set the benchmark’s upper limits—peaking at 45.23% semantic and 40.43% temporal accuracy—but suffer from severe processing delays (4.23s–5.51s). Token merging (CaM-like Zhang et al. (2024)) offers a middle ground, cutting pruning latency in half ( 2.33s–2.87s) while remaining competitive. Finally, external retrieval strategies like ReKV Di et al. (2025) and full StreamingTOM Chen et al. (2025b) reveal that quantized offloading is beneficial for long-horizon memory; it rescues ultra-long recall (reaching 34.21% for StreamingTOM) and slashes processing time (down to 1.43s), albeit with a slight dip in average accuracy. Ultimately, while current SOTA methods successfully specialize in different memory profiles, all still operate well below 1 FPS, highlighting that achieving true real-time streaming ingestion remains an open challenge.

5.3 Semantic Profiles and Temporal Decay

Figure 5 shows that merging, pruning and offloading techniques have different effects across semantic categories and temporal recall regimes. While all improve over baselines, pruning-based methods often have advantages, especially in the temporal and detail categories, and offloading-based approaches achieve better results on social and in medium-long to ultra-long recall. Overall, these results highlight the importance of evaluating across semantic categories and recall times, rather than just by aggregate accuracies.

5.4 Memory Budget

Table 5 shows that memory budget is a driver of accuracy, but with diminishing returns. Increasing the budget from 2.6K to 9.8K tokens, from Row 5 to Row 5, raises semantic accuracy from 40.88% to 45.19% and temporal accuracy from 35.59% to 40.43%. Larger budgets further improve the averages, peaking at 47.08% semantic and 41.94% temporal with 50.8K tokens in Row 5, but nearly triple processing time relative to the smallest budget in Row 5.

6 Conclusion and Limitations

EgoStream establishes a diagnostic benchmark and unified framework for evaluating streaming episodic memory in egocentric vision. By introducing the Answer Validity Window (AVW) to decouple genuine forgetting from natural scene changes, our evaluations reveal that comparable aggregate accuracies often mask distinct memory vulnerabilities. Moving beyond simple performance metrics, EgoStream provides a precise tool to diagnose exactly what, and for how long, embodied systems remember—laying the groundwork for reliable, context-aware assistive agents.

Limitations and Societal Impact EgoStream establishes a foundation benchmark for streaming episodic memory, but several limitations remain. Although we provide robust baselines, memory decay may vary across backbones and implementations. While EgoStream can support open-ended QA, we focus on multiple choice, leaving free-form generation unexplored. Finally, EgoStream inherits environmental and geographic biases from its source datasets and narrations. Streaming episodic memory may benefit assistive technologies, but also raises privacy and surveillance risks by capturing bystanders or sensitive interactions; these risks require mitigation before deployment.
